docs.title: The Anatomy Theatre
docs.text:
(a working title — the anatomy theatre was the room where the anatomy lesson was taught)

This is a reading library: a small number of subjects, each built out to the depth of a good textbook. Every subject opens with an overview and a recommended reading path, then chapters you can read in order or dip into, then deep dives wherever there is real material to go further — the intent is that you can always dig a little deeper, and never hit filler.

Subjects:

  • Dance — choreographers and their works, movement vocabularies and how machines might learn them, notation, the music relationship, chance and algorithmic methods, costume and the staged body, and the fully synthetic dancer. First chapters live; more arriving in batches.
  • Minimal techno — the production craft: groove, the voices, reduction, long-form hypnosis, the artists' documented methods. Queued.

Sources and provenance sit behind tap-able footnotes at the bottom of each page — the text stays clean. Everything here is distilled from a private knowledge commons plus the general knowledge of the agents who write it; where a page draws on the commons' research notes, it says so in a collapsed Field notes block at the end.

docs.title: Dance
docs.text: Choreography solved a problem seventy years before anyone asked a machine to: how to build a limited vocabulary of movement and a set of rules that recombine it into something worth watching. This subject covers the art form whole — the traditions and their makers, the languages of movement and the systems for writing them down, the strange marriage with music, the chance procedures and algorithms, the dressed and lit body on a stage, and the fully synthetic dancer — but that solved problem is its center of gravity, and the chapters radiate out from it.

docs.title: The shape of the subject
docs.text:
Eight parts. Chapters are self-contained — you can read any one cold — but within a part they're ordered, and the parts themselves zoom from the territory down to the machinery:

  • I · The territory — what dance is and what it's for; a world atlas of everything anyone calls dance; ballet's long history; the modern revolt; street and club styles. (coming)
  • II · Movement language — how vocabularies of movement get built, taught, described, and — the open frontier — discovered by machines from video. (complete)
  • III · Writing it down — Labanotation, Benesh, motif notation; video and digital scores. (coming)
  • IV · Music and dance — both directions of the marriage: choreographers using music, composers writing for bodies. (coming)
  • V · Chance, systems, algorithms — Cunningham to code: the generative tradition and the architecture it converged on. (complete)
  • VI · The staged body — costume, props, environment, light. (coming)
  • VII · The synthetic dancer — the plausible body, motion capture, movement generation, rendering. (first chapter below)
  • VIII · The shelf — reference pages on the choreographers themselves. (coming)

docs.title: Available now
docs.text:
Movement language (read in order, or dip in):

  • Codified vocabularies — what happens when a tradition names its movements: ballet's lexicon, the mudra systems, hula, flamenco, and the street's uninstitutional canon.
  • Technique as vocabulary — modern dance's alternative: build a training system that produces a body, and let the body be the vocabulary.
  • The craft: composition best practices — Humphrey's principles, phrase-craft, the rehearsal room, editing, and Lerman's feedback protocol.
  • Building a gamut — how a piece-specific movement vocabulary is actually assembled: units, state, operators, and the traps between them.
  • Effort and quality — Laban's answer to a question most vocabularies forget to ask: not what the body does, but how.
  • Machine-discovered vocabularies — can a machine find the units from video, unsupervised? Yes for poses and segments, not yet for named, typed units — what works, and what a working pipeline would look like.

Chance, systems, algorithms:

  • Chance and rule-based choreography — Cunningham's coin tosses, Brown's accumulations, Childs's permutations, Halprin's cycles: what seventy years of generative choreography actually did, and the two-layer architecture all of it shares.
  • The gamut+rules architecture — the engineering synthesis: transition legality, the three transition policies, the human gate, and why the rendering of a machine's proposal is a design decision.
  • Computational choreography: a history — thirty-five years of choreographers composing with computers, LifeForms to AISOMA, and the five patterns that held the whole way.
  • Choreographing in latent spaces — the continuous counter-position: learned motion manifolds, their pre-mathematical ancestors, and what survives the loss of the unit.

The synthetic dancer:

  • The captured body: video to skeleton to animation — the state of the art and the free tooling for extracting 3D dance from video, and the clever repairs (learned priors, physics simulation) that make the result look alive.

Plates — contemplation pages: one dense structure, laid out for staring at, not reading:

  • Plate I · The Movement Alphabet

docs.title: Building a gamut
docs.text:
Choreographers rarely make dances out of "movement" in general. They make a gamut — a finite, named set of movement units built for one piece — and then compose with that. The word is Cunningham's, borrowed from music, and the practice is close to universal even among choreographers who'd never use the term: Trisha Brown's Primary Accumulation is thirty movements; Cunningham's Torse is sixty-four phrases expanded from five torso positions; Lucinda Childs built entire works from a single step pattern permuted through space. If you've ever designed a synth patch bank for one track, or a constrained palette for one visual piece, you know the move: the vocabulary is a composition decision, made before composing begins.

This chapter is about how that vocabulary gets built well — which turns out to be a genuine design discipline with named failure modes, most of them invisible until you try to recombine the units and things break. The dance tradition worked these problems out by hand over decades; the same lessons apply directly if the thing recombining your units is a rule system or a model.

docs.title: Start from a coverage checklist, not from taste
docs.text:
The naive way to build a vocabulary is to improvise material until you have "enough," then name what you kept. The predictable result is a set that clusters around its author's habits — twenty units that are secretly five, all sharing a dynamic range, a level, a relationship to weight. Any generator downstream (human or machine) can then only recombine within that cluster.

The corrective is an independent checklist of movement classes, scored against your set. The best-established one is Ann Hutchinson Guest's Movement Alphabet1: a claimed-complete list of fifteen "prime actions from which all movement derives," in six groups — any action, stillness · flexion, extension, rotation · travelling, direction · support, spring · balance, falling · motion toward, motion away, destination, any form of relating. Treat completeness as a strong pedagogical claim rather than a theorem (it has been taught for forty years, which counts for something), and it becomes exactly what a vocabulary-builder needs: fill the empty cells, and your set spans the space of movement instead of sampling one corner. (The alphabet also has a plate — the fifteen classes laid out visually, for exactly the kind of staring the list rewards.)

Look closely at the list, though, and five of the fifteen aren't performable actions at all. Motion toward, motion away, destination, and form of relating are specification modes — ways of defining a movement (by its trajectory, by its endpoint, by its relationship) rather than movements themselves. Strip those out and the performable core is about ten verb classes: travel, turn, spring, gesture into a direction, flex, extend, transfer weight, balance, fall, be still. Ten verbs sounds small. It's the right order of magnitude — the historical gamuts that worked are all counted in dozens, never hundreds, a point the systems chapters return to with the receipts.

docs.title: State-changing verbs must be first-class units
docs.text:
The subtlest thing about Guest's alphabet is what it chooses to promote. Support (a weight transfer), balance, and falling are alphabet entries — full verbs — rather than adverbs or transitions hiding between other moves. That looks like a taxonomic quirk and is actually the deepest design rule in the chapter:

anything that changes state that other units will read deserves its own named unit.

Fall is the canonical case. A fall isn't just a shape in time — it writes state: the body ends off-balance, with momentum, and only certain movements can legally happen next. If your vocabulary treats falling as something that just happens inside transitions, no rule system can see that state, and sequences will be generated that a body cannot perform. Worse, falls create an obligation: for every direction your vocabulary can fall, it needs at least one recovery unit that reads the off-balance state and resolves it. A vocabulary with falls and no recoveries deadlocks — the generator paints the dancer into corners.

This is a special case of a distinction worth making for the whole set: which units are atomic (self-contained, no dependencies — a gesture, a turn in place) and which are entangled (they read or write state that other units depend on — falls, catches, weight transfers, anything with momentum). Atomic units can be recombined freely. Entangled units need their dependencies declared, or recombination breaks in ways that only show up two units downstream. Map this before composing, not after.

And one more promotion from the alphabet worth honoring: stillness is an item, not a gap. A rest is a unit with duration, level, and shape — Cage's lesson transplanted to the body. It also happens to be the single most useful edit point when movement is destined for camera, which is worth remembering the moment your dancers are synthetic.

docs.title: Give every unit a type signature
docs.text:
The practical form of "declare the dependencies" is borrowed from programming: give each unit a type signature — what it requires to begin (preconditions) and what's true when it ends (postconditions). For movement, six fields cover the state that matters:

Field What it records support which base bears weight — feet, one foot, seat, back, hands+feet… level floor / low / mid / standing / air balance balanced, suspended, off-balance (and which way) momentum magnitude and direction, including rotational facing relative orientation change, never absolute free limbs what's available for the next unit to use

Then unit B may follow unit A exactly when A's postconditions satisfy B's preconditions, field by field, with wildcards where a unit genuinely doesn't care. Legality stops being a judgment call and becomes checkable by inspection — which is the entire foundation the gamut+rules architecture builds on.

Two field-specific notes, both earned the hard way. Weight is the treacherous field: dance pedagogy independently names incomplete weight transfer as the root cause of most transition failures, so annotate support changes with special care. And facing must be stored relative — a unit that "ends facing stage left" is really a unit that ends rotated 90° from where it began; store the absolute version and you'll reject joins that were fine and duplicate units to compensate.

One honest caveat from the notation world: every system surveyed, Guest's included, carries a standing bias. If floorwork matters to your vocabulary — and in contemporary movement it will — don't inherit a default support list; name the floor supports explicitly (back, side, seat, hands-and-feet) as first-class values.

docs.title: The operator layer: transforms, not more units
docs.text:
A gamut of a few dozen units would exhaust itself quickly if units were all there was. The second layer is operators: transformations applied to units to generate variants. Dance pedagogy converged on a remarkably stable catalog decades ago — Blom & Chaplin's sixteen ways to manipulate a motif2 (repetition, retrograde, inversion, size, tempo, rhythm, quality, instrumentation, force, background, staging, embellishment, change of level, additive, fragmentation, combination), with William Forsythe's ~thirty geometric operations — extension, extrusion, folding, bridging, avoidance, reorientation, compression — as the improvisation-side twin.3

The structural fact that matters more than either list: operators are material-independent. Forsythe's catalog reads like a graphics API precisely because it applies to whatever the dancer already knows — the vocabulary and the operator set are orthogonal layers. That's why roughly thirty concepts constitute a literacy a practitioner internalizes rather than a repertoire they memorize, and it's the standard to hold your own operators to: an operator that only works on one unit isn't an operator, it's a variant that snuck into the wrong layer.

Two constraints keep an operator layer sound:

  • Closure — applying any operator to legal material must yield legal material. An operator that can produce output outside the vocabulary's own rules poisons everything downstream.
  • Survivability — the operand must remain itself under the transform. A reaching curve compresses beautifully; a walking step compresses into nonsense. Part of authoring a unit is knowing which operators it survives.

docs.title: Not all operators are equally automatable
docs.text:
If a rule system (or an agent) will be applying these operators, the catalog needs one more sorting: by mechanizability — how much judgment the operator secretly requires. The sixteen sort cleanly into three tiers:

  • Tier 1 — fully mechanical. Repetition ×n, tempo change including freeze, re-facing and relocation, level transposition, mirroring, size augmentation/diminution, retrograde. Safe to auto-apply.
  • Tier 2 — mechanical plus a light curation pass. Fragmentation (take the first, middle, or last third), re-accenting within the same duration, flipping one effort quality bit, instrumentation (move the phrase to a different body part — undefined for weight-bearing units), appending an ornament.
  • Tier 3 — judgment-heavy. Whole-quality reimagining, inversion, redesigning the background behind a motif, stacking several operators at once. Offer these as prompts to a human; don't auto-apply them.

The tiering isn't invented — it's empirical. Every teaching syllabus carries tiers 1–2; only the full scholarly catalog carries tier 3. And it comes with a trap worth framing on the wall: mechanizable to specify is not the same as feasible to execute. Retrograde is the cleanest tier-1 operator on paper and one of the hardest things a body can be asked to do with any unit that bears weight or carries momentum — playing a fall backwards is not a fall. A catalog inherited from pedagogy encodes what a trained human can be asked to attempt, not what a generator can safely emit; check every "mechanical" operator against the physics before trusting its tier, and restrict the rough ones to gesture-dominant material.

docs.title: What a finished gamut looks like
docs.text:
Pulling the threads together, a well-built gamut is:

  1. Small — dozens of units, chosen, not harvested;
  2. Spanning — scored against an independent class list, empty cells filled deliberately;
  3. Stateful — state-changing verbs promoted to first-class units, entanglements mapped, every fall paired with recoveries;
  4. Typed — each unit carrying pre/postconditions over support, level, balance, momentum, relative facing, free limbs;
  5. Transformable — a separate, closed operator layer, tiered by how much judgment each operator hides.

None of this yet says how units get sequenced, what makes a chain of them legal in practice, or who judges the result — that's the architecture chapter. And the question of how a unit is performed, as opposed to what it is, has its own axis entirely: effort and quality, next.

  2. Anne Green Gilbert–era pedagogy standardized many operator lists, but the canonical sixteen are from Lynne Anne Blom & L. Tarin Chaplin, The Intimate Act of Choreography (1982) — still the standard composition textbook. ↩

  3. William Forsythe, Improvisation Technologies: A Tool for the Analytical Dance Eye (ZKM, 1999) — the CD-ROM in which Forsythe draws his operations as white lines over video of his own body; it reappears in the digital-scores chapter. ↩

docs.title: Codified vocabularies
docs.text:
Before any question about generating movement comes a stranger fact worth sitting with: several of the world's dance traditions long ago did to movement what language did to sound. They drew boundaries in the continuous flow of the body, named the segments, and built a culture of transmission on the names. A ballet class in Tokyo, Buenos Aires, and Paris runs on the same French words; a bharatanatyam dancer's hands speak a gesture lexicon fixed in treatises two thousand years old; a b-boy's six-step is as precisely specified as a tendu, with no academy anywhere in sight.

This chapter is about what codification is, what it buys, what it costs, and how differently it can be governed — questions that turn out to matter enormously the moment you want a machine anywhere near choreography, because a codified vocabulary is, among other things, a dataset with labels.

docs.title: Ballet: the state-sponsored lexicon
docs.text:
The deepest codification project in Western dance began as absolutist politics. Louis XIV — a serious dancer who performed as the sun in Ballet de la Nuit — chartered the Académie Royale de Danse in 1661, and his ballet master Pierre Beauchamp fixed the five positions of the feet that still open every ballet class on earth. By 1700, Raoul-Auger Feuillet had published Chorégraphie — the word originally named a notation system — and the French terms were on paper: plié, tendu, jeté, arabesque, pirouette.1

Today the working lexicon runs to a few hundred named steps, and the names are doing at least four jobs at once. Transmission: the vocabulary crossed three centuries and every border without losing definition. Correction: a teacher can say "your arabesque is behind your shoulder" only because arabesque picks out a thing with a right way to be. Chunking: a dancer's working memory holds a phrase as six names, not six hundred joint angles — the same compression trick as chess players seeing structures instead of pieces. Assessment: entire examination systems (the Royal Academy of Dance syllabus, the Vaganova method's graded levels) exist because the units are enumerable.

Note what the lexicon deliberately excludes, though — a detail the gamut chapter should make ring loudly. Ballet names its positions and steps, but the connective tissue between them lives in the training, not the list. And note that ballet is not one vocabulary but a family of dialects: Vaganova, Cecchetti, French school, Balanchine's American inflection — same core lexicon, systematically different accents, arms, and musicality. Vocabularies drift, even policed ones.

docs.title: The mudra systems: when gestures mean
docs.text:
Indian classical dance codified earlier, deeper, and toward a different end. The Natya Shastra — the Sanskrit performance treatise compiled somewhere around the turn of the first millennium — and the later Abhinaya Darpana specify the hasta mudras: twenty-eight single-hand gestures plus around two dozen two-hand combinations, each named, each specified finger by finger, each carrying meanings.2 Pataka (the flat hand) can be a forest, a river, denial, or a slap, depending on context and placement; the same physical sign is reused across semantic fields the way a phoneme is.

This is the crucial difference from ballet: bharatanatyam's vocabulary is semantic. The tradition splits its own practice into nritta — pure dance, rhythm and geometry, built from unit steps called adavus (about a dozen families, over a hundred variants, drilled like scales) — and abhinaya, expressive narration, where the mudras function as a sign language telling stories from the epics. A single dancer narrates: gods, demons, lovers, weather. Ballet's names point at shapes; the mudras point at the world.

Hawaiian hula sits in the same family with a different emphasis: the hands depict — moon, wave, cliff, rain — but the dance exists to carry the mele, the chant; movement is the memory palace of an oral literature. Transmission is institutional but familial: the hālau (school) under a kumu hula, lineages guarded like archives, because for centuries the dance largely was the archive.

docs.title: Flamenco: a grammar with few nouns
docs.text:
Flamenco is the instructive counterexample: a rigorously codified tradition with surprisingly few named units. What's fixed is the palo — the song form, with its compás (the rhythmic cycle, like the twelve-beat of soleá) — and a set of structural events: the llamada (the dancer's call for attention), the remate (the phrase-closing punctuation), the desplante. The movement material itself — braceo (arm work), floreo (wrist and finger circling), zapateado (footwork) — is described by manner more than enumerated by name. A bailaora doesn't execute step #47; she improvises within compás, in conversation with singer and guitarist, deploying a personal vocabulary shaped by convention.

Flamenco codifies the frame and leaves the material personal — the exact inverse of ballet, and a live demonstration of the frame-versus-realization split the chance chapter found running through jazz, raga, and Cunningham alike. A vocabulary, it turns out, can live in the nouns or in the grammar.

docs.title: The street: canon without an academy
docs.text:
The most remarkable codification story is the most recent, because it happened with no academy, no state, no notation, and no tuition — and produced a vocabulary as stable as any of them.

Breaking, born in the Bronx in the 1970s, organized itself into a canon any practitioner worldwide can recite: toprock (standing opener), downrock (floorwork — the six-step is its scale exercise, as codified as any adavu), freezes (held shapes — baby freeze, chair), power moves (windmill, flare, headspin). Popping arrived from Fresno with Boogaloo Sam and the Electric Boogaloos carrying its own named techniques — the pop itself, waving, tutting; locking from Don Campbell in LA — the lock, points, wrist rolls. Each with named founders, named moves, and ferociously maintained boundaries (conflating popping and locking, or calling any of it "breakdancing," marks an outsider instantly).

The governance mechanism is the cypher and the battle: canon is maintained by competitive consensus — you bite (copy without transformation), the circle knows; you innovate on the foundation, the circle ratifies it, and your move may enter the canon with your name attached. Transmission ran through crews and VHS tapes, then YouTube, which acted as an accidental global academy — and the whole arc reached a surreal milestone when breaking, an art form born on cardboard, debuted at the Paris Olympics in 2024, judging criteria and all. Institutions came to the vocabulary, half a century after the vocabulary organized itself without them.

docs.title: What codification buys, costs, and decides
docs.text:
Lay the traditions side by side and the anatomy of codification comes clear.

What naming buys is the same everywhere: chunking (working memory holds names, not joint angles), correction (you can only fix what you can point at), transmission across time and distance, assessment, and — subtlest — remix affordance: units with names and boundaries can be recombined, quoted, and taught out of order. Every generative system in Part V is downstream of this property.

What it costs is thinkability. A vocabulary is a hypothesis about which distinctions matter, and it quietly makes everything between its entries harder to see, teach, or ask for. Ballet's lexicon has no word for most of what Pina Bausch put on stage. This cost is real enough that an entire century of dance — the next chapter — is best read as a series of responses to it, and one of them (Gaga) responds by refusing names on principle.

And someone decides. An académie under royal charter, a sabha of gurus and treatises, a family lineage, a cypher's rolling consensus — each governance model produces a different kind of vocabulary: ballet's is precise and slow-moving; the street's is precise and fast, absorbing innovation in years rather than generations; flamenco's guards the grammar and frees the nouns. When you build a vocabulary of your own — a gamut — you are implicitly choosing a governance model too, even if the whole académie is you.

docs.text: title: The craft: composition best practices summary: The documented working wisdom of making dances — Humphrey's principles, phrase-craft, rehearsal practice, editing, and Lerman's feedback protocol. covers: []

docs.title: The craft: composition best practices
docs.text:
Every art accumulates a layer of working wisdom that isn't theory and isn't technique — the things experienced makers tell you at the point where your piece is almost working. Dance is unusually lucky here: its craft lore got written down, by masters, and two texts tower over the genre. Doris Humphrey's The Art of Making Dances (1959) is the canon — the distilled judgment of a first-generation modern choreographer, finished just before her death, and still the book working choreographers actually quote.1 Lynne Anne Blom and L. Tarin Chaplin's The Intimate Act of Choreography (1982) is the standard classroom companion. Add one modern protocol for feedback and you have this chapter: best practices, as documented practice.

Fair warning about the genre: craft rules are compressions of experience, not laws. Every rule below has been productively broken by someone in the shelf. What makes them worth learning anyway is that each one names a failure mode you will otherwise discover expensively — and that they translate, with almost embarrassing directness, into design heuristics for anyone building a system that composes.

docs.title: Humphrey's physics of attention
docs.text:
The most quoted part of Humphrey's book is the blunt checklist near its end, and the items earn their fame:

Symmetry is lifeless. Two-dimensional design is lifeless. The eye is faster than the ear. All dances are too long. A good ending is forty per cent of the dance. Monotony is fatal; look for contrasts. Don't be a slave to, or a mutilator of, the music. Don't intellectualize; motivate movement. Don't leave the ending to the end.

What reads like aphorism is really a physics of audience attention, and it repays unpacking.

Symmetry is lifeless because a symmetric stage picture resolves — nothing is owed, nothing impends. Asymmetry is unfinished business, and unfinished business is watchable. (Her corollary: symmetry spends meaningfully when you want stability, ceremony, an ending — it's lifeless as a default, potent as a choice.)

The eye is faster than the ear — visual pattern is grasped almost instantly, where musical pattern needs time to unfold. Practical consequence: movement repeated as often as its accompanying music becomes boring sooner; the eye finished earlier. Any system that varies music and movement on the same schedule has this exactly wrong.

The stage itself has physics. Humphrey mapped the proscenium stage as a field of unequal forces: center stage is power; upstage center is remote majesty (entrances of gods and queens); downstage corners are intimate and confessional; the diagonals are the strongest travel paths. You can defy the map, but the audience reads by it either way — placement is never neutral.

All dances are too long needs no unpacking. It is the single most confirmed observation in the history of the art form.

A good ending is forty per cent of the dance — and don't leave the ending to the end: design it early, because everything before it is, structurally, approach. An ending discovered in the final rehearsal week reads exactly like one.

docs.title: Phrase-craft
docs.text:
Blom and Chaplin's classroom contribution starts smaller: the phrase as the basic unit of composition — a span of movement with a beginning, a development, and an arrival, most naturally sized to a breath. Their craft rules cluster around two disciplines:

Shape the phrase's energy deliberately. A phrase has a dynamic arc — where it peaks, how it ends (a punctuating accent versus a dissolve versus a suspension that hands momentum to the next phrase). Uniform arcs are the phrase-level version of Humphrey's monotony warning, and the effort chapter's anti-monotony rule — never more than two consecutive phrases with the same effort signature — is the same discipline made mechanical.

Develop before you invent. Their deepest advice, and the least intuitive for beginners: when a piece feels thin, the reflex is new material, and the reflex is almost always wrong. A dance usually needs less material, more thoroughly explored — which is what the operator catalog is for. The sixteen manipulations exist so that one good motif can honestly fill ten minutes. A piece built from six ideas lightly touched reads as a variety show; a piece built from one idea genuinely developed reads as a world. (The chance chapter's gamut sizes — always dozens, never hundreds — are this same judgment, measured.)

docs.title: The rehearsal room
docs.text:
The craft of making is distinct from the craft of the made thing, and modern practice has conventions worth naming plainly.

Dances are made on bodies, not on paper. The near-universal contemporary method is to bring structures, tasks, and images into the studio and develop material on the specific dancers — whose bodies, histories, and offers shape the result so strongly that a work re-set on a new cast is understood to be a translation. The purest version is tasking: give the dancers a generative problem ("phrase A backwards at half tempo while descending"; "a solo that never leaves the wall's shadow") and curate what comes back. A choreographer running tasks is, in this subject's terms, precisely a sequencer plus a human gate — the dancers are the generator, and the craft is in the task design and the selection.

Video replaced notation as working memory. The universal modern habit: film everything, because tomorrow nobody — including the choreographer — fully remembers today's material. (What video doesn't capture is the subject of the notation chapters, coming.)

Marking is a tool, not a failure. Dancers rehearse structure at reduced energy ("marking") to save bodies; choreographers must see full-out runs to judge dynamics, because — Humphrey again — movement reads slower and weaker from the house than it feels on the floor.

docs.title: Editing, and the outside eye
docs.text:
Humphrey's "all dances are too long" implies the discipline: cutting is where pieces are made. The craft lore here is identical to every other art's — kill your darlings; the section you love most is the first suspect — with one dance-specific sharpening: length errors are usually repetition-count errors. The material is right; it happens four times instead of two. (Recall the eye's speed.)

Because the maker's eye adapts — you cannot see your piece by week six — mature practice builds in an outside eye. At the institutional end this is the dance dramaturg (Pina Bausch's Raimund Hoghe is the famous case; Anne Teresa De Keersmaeker has worked with Bojana Cvejić): a professional watcher whose job is the piece's logic, not its steps. At the collegial end it's a trusted colleague at a late run-through. Either way the principle is the same: fresh perception is a resource the maker cannot self-supply.

docs.title: Feedback: the Lerman protocol
docs.text:
Which raises the hardest craft problem in any collaborative art: how to receive opinions without surrendering the work. Dance's canonical answer — now exported to theaters, art schools, and writing workshops everywhere — is choreographer Liz Lerman's Critical Response Process, a four-step structure for feedback sessions:2

  1. Statements of meaning. Responders say what was meaningful, evocative, striking — before any evaluation. (The artist learns what actually landed, which is data no opinion contains.)
  2. The artist asks. The artist questions the responders — about the passages they are unsure of, on their agenda, not the room's.
  3. Neutral questions. Responders may ask genuinely neutral questions ("what governed the costume choice?" — not "why was the costume grey?", which smuggles a verdict). Forming a truly neutral question forces the responder to locate their reaction before broadcasting it.
  4. Permissioned opinions. "I have an opinion about the ending — would you like to hear it?" The artist may decline.

The design insight is that CRP treats the artist's continued authority over the work as the resource to protect — unsolicited fixes are the failure mode, because they quietly transfer authorship to the loudest responder. Readers of the architecture chapter will recognize the structure: CRP is a human gate with a designed protocol, engineered so the gatekeeper stays the artist.

docs.title: The craft table, translated
docs.text:
Because this library's reader builds generative systems, the translation deserves to be explicit. Each craft rule is a system heuristic wearing rehearsal clothes:

Craft rule System analogue All dances are too long Aggressive length priors; generate short, extend only on evidence Symmetry is lifeless (by default) Penalize resolved/symmetric states except at designated cadences The eye is faster than the ear Visual material needs a faster variation schedule than its music Design the ending early Plan form backward from the ending, not forward from the opening Monotony is fatal Enforce contrast floors (the effort-signature rule, mechanized) Develop before you invent Exhaust the operator catalog before enlarging the gamut Stage geography Placement priors — position carries meaning before movement starts The outside eye Fresh-judge evaluation: never validate on the maker's adapted eye Critical Response Process Gate protocol: meaning-data first, opinions by permission, artist keeps authority

None of this replaces judgment — Humphrey's whole book is a plea for judgment against formula. But it is the accumulated record of where judgment usually errs, and that, for makers and for system-builders alike, is exactly what best practices are.

Field notes

The effort-signature contrast rule renders theory-laban-effort-quality-axis's pedagogy heuristic (covered in the effort chapter); the develop-before-invent principle is the human-craft face of structure-operator-mechanizability-tiers and structure-gamut-plus-sequencer.

  2. Liz Lerman & John Borstel, Liz Lerman's Critical Response Process (2003). Lerman developed the protocol within her Dance Exchange company in the 1990s; it is now institutional practice far beyond dance. ↩

docs.title: Effort and quality
docs.text:
Watch two dancers perform the same phrase — same steps, same counts, same shapes — and you can still see, instantly, that they are doing different things. One presses through the movement as if the air were honey; the other flicks through it like shooing insects. Everything in the previous chapter — units, signatures, operators — describes what the body does. This chapter is about the axis that describes how, which turns out to be separable from the what, nameable, and — the reason it earns a chapter — astonishingly well-engineered.

The engineering is Rudolf Laban's. A Hungarian-born movement theorist working in Weimar Germany and later wartime England, Laban built the twentieth century's most systematic analysis of human movement — Labanotation, the symbolic score system, is his (it gets its own chapter), and so is the analytical framework now taught as Laban Movement Analysis. The piece of it that matters here is the category he called Effort: a factored decomposition of movement quality, the dynamic, expressive dimension that survives when you subtract the choreography.1

docs.title: Four factors, two poles each
docs.text:
Laban's claim is that quality decomposes into four independent bipolar factors, each of which he tied to an inner attitude:

Factor Poles Inner attitude Space direct ↔ indirect attention Weight strong ↔ light intention Time sudden ↔ sustained decision Flow bound ↔ free progression

Direct movement channels toward a single point (a dart's flight); indirect attends everywhere at once (a fly's). Strong engages weight forcefully; light nearly denies it. Sudden is urgent, sustained is unhurried. Bound flow can be stopped at any instant; free flow is committed — launched, ballistic, unstoppable without a recovery.

Any factored system invites the same question you'd ask of a synth: what do the combinations sound like? Take the first three factors as binary and you get eight combinations, and this is where Laban's system shows its craftsmanship — all eight have names, and the names are vivid enough to teach:

sudden, direct sudden, indirect sustained, direct sustained, indirect strong punch slash press wring light dab flick glide float

These are the eight effort actions, and the table above is the canonical assignment — worth stating plainly because actor-training materials garble it constantly.2 Each name is a compressed lesson: you already know, in your arm, the difference between wring (strong, sustained, indirect — a towel) and press (strong, sustained, direct — a stamp), and that kinesthetic memory is doing the work a paragraph of description would fail at.

docs.title: The cube, and distance for free
docs.text:
Now the property that makes Effort more than a nice taxonomy. Three binary factors put the eight actions on the corners of a cube — and cube adjacency is a metric. Two actions differing in one factor are neighbors: punch → press changes only Time, and reads as development, a modulation of the same idea. Flip all three factors — punch → float — and you have maximal contrast, the movement equivalent of a subito pianissimo.

If you build generative systems, that sentence should have lit up: this is a modifier axis that ships with its own distance function. "Vary it a little" versus "contrast hard" stops being a taste call and becomes a Hamming distance — 1 bit is development, 3 bits is rupture. The pedagogy even hands you an anti-monotony rule ready for mechanization: never let more than two consecutive phrases share an effort signature. That's a constraint a rule system can enforce while remaining wholly agnostic about which movements it's shaping — a dynamic arc drawn with no new machinery at all.

And it layers cleanly. The proof is a computer-animation classic: the EMOTE model implemented Effort as four continuous dials in [−1, +1] that modulate the timing curves and trajectory shape of independently authored base gestures.3 Quality as a pure multiplier over material defined elsewhere — the modifier ideal from the operator layer, demonstrated at animation-production quality in the year 2000. When a vocabulary keeps what and how in separate layers, one gamut of a few dozen units times eight qualities times a couple of intensity levels yields a combinatorial space in the thousands, every point of it nameable.

docs.title: Flow is not like the others
docs.text:
You'll have noticed the eight actions use only three factors. Flow, the fourth, is deliberately excluded — and the reason generalizes into a design rule.

Bound flow means the movement can be arrested at any moment; free flow means it can't — the dancer has committed momentum that must land somewhere. That isn't a color of the movement. It's a postcondition: a fact about what can legally happen next. A free-flow leap doesn't merely feel different from a bound-flow reach — it constrains the successor unit in a way no quality should. Which is why Flow belongs in the type signature — in the momentum and balance fields of the unit's pre/post contract, feeding the transition checks of the architecture chapter — while Weight, Time, and Space stay in the palette as pure style.

The rule underneath: when a "quality" changes what may follow, it isn't a quality — it's state. Sort your axes by that test and both layers stay honest.

docs.title: What effort is not
docs.text:
Two boundaries keep the system from being oversold.

Effort values are performance targets, not measurables. Inter-rater reliability between trained Laban observers is only moderate; no checker, human or algorithmic, can verify that a movement was performed with "wringing" quality. This isn't a flaw to engineer away — it defines where the axis lives. In the division of labor the gamut+rules chapter makes precise, mechanical state — support, level, momentum — is the machine's tier, and quality is irreducibly the human's tier: a target you set, a judgment you render, never a value you assert was achieved.

The vocabulary is a convention, not the only one. Modern-dance pedagogy commonly teaches six movement qualities instead — sustained, percussive, swinging, suspended, collapsing, vibratory — and Ohad Naharin's Gaga (his movement language for Batsheva) works in texture words: float, quake, melt, groove. Both map, roughly, onto the same underlying axis Laban factored. The practical advice: pick the naming your performers already speak; keep the cube underneath for the machinery.

docs.title: The transferable lesson
docs.text:
Strip away the dance and Effort is a masterclass in designing any modifier axis: prefer a product of a few binary factors over a flat list of adjectives. A flat adjective list — "make it aggressive, dreamy, punchy, mellow…" — grows without structure, overlaps without warning, and gives you no notion of near or far. A factored product gives you orthogonality by construction, a built-in distance metric, and — if you name the corners well — memorable handles that teach themselves. Eight named cells from three bits is a better interface than thirty unstructured adjectives, whether the thing being modified is a phrase of movement, a synth patch, or a generated shot.

Laban got there in the 1940s, for bodies. It has yet to be improved on.

Field notes

This chapter renders the commons note theory-laban-effort-quality-axis (the effort cube as a modifier axis with a free contrast metric; Flow as type-signature state; EMOTE as layerability proof; quality as performance target, not measurable).

  1. Laban's own presentation is The Mastery of Movement (1950, revised with Lisa Ullmann); Effort was first systematized with F. C. Lawrence in Effort (1947), a wartime study of industrial movement efficiency — the factory floor, oddly, is where the expressive vocabulary was forged. ↩

  2. "Punch" appears in some sources as "thrust" — same cell, same action. ↩

  3. Diane Chi, Monica Costa, Liwei Zhao & Norman Badler, "The EMOTE Model for Effort and Shape," SIGGRAPH 2000. Badler's Center for Human Modeling and Simulation at Penn spent decades making Laban computable. ↩

docs.title: Machine-discovered vocabularies
docs.text:
Everything so far in this part has had a human building the vocabulary — naming it like ballet, training it into bodies like Graham, assembling it by hand like a gamut. The question this chapter takes seriously is whether the building itself can be delegated: point a model at hours of dance video and ask it to find the units — no labels, no choreographer, no Movement Alphabet — the way one might hope a model would find the phonemes of an unfamiliar language from raw speech.

The honest headline for mid-2026: yes, at the level of recurring poses and recurring short segments — and no, at the level of named, typed, performable units. The machine finds clusters; a human still decides what is a unit. That gap is the interesting part, and understanding exactly where it sits is what lets you build a pipeline that uses discovery for what it's good at. Let me take the field apart by stages and by method family, then say plainly what a working system would look like.

docs.title: The pipeline, in four stages
docs.text:
Every discovery approach decomposes the same way:

  • Capture — video to skeleton, the business of the captured-body chapter: 2D keypoints or, better, world-grounded 3D bodies.
  • Tokenize or segment — turn the continuous skeleton stream into candidate pieces: either quantize each moment into a finite set of codes, or find boundaries that cut the stream into segments.
  • Cluster — group the pieces into recurring types, so that "this kind of thing" becomes a countable category.
  • Name and type — give the categories names a dancer can use and signatures a rule system can check. This is the stage no published method performs.

The first three stages have real, working literature. The fourth is the human gate, and it has not moved.

docs.title: Family one: codebooks of poses
docs.text:
The dominant method is the VQ-VAE — a vector-quantized autoencoder. Train a network to compress a short window of pose through a bottleneck, but force the bottleneck to pick its value from a finite codebook of learned entries. Every moment of movement is then represented by an index into that codebook, and each codebook entry — each code — is a discovered unit pose.

The dance-specific proof is Bailando (2022), a music-to-dance system whose authors named its vocabulary component with unusual candor: the choreographic memory.1 Its design choices are worth reading as vocabulary decisions:

  • It trains separate codebooks for the upper and lower body, so any dance becomes a sequence of paired codes — a limb-instrumentation split, made structural.
  • The learned codes are human-interpretable: the paper shows them, and they read as recognizable dancing-style poses, discovered with no labels at all.
  • A GPT then composes codes into sequences conditioned on music, with an actor-critic term rewarding beat alignment — and the authors sell the whole thing as interpretability: "the choreography process becomes selecting and sorting the quantized positions from the choreographic memory, instead of a black box."

Hold that last sentence; it's going to matter.

The general motion-tokenizer lineage — built for text-to-motion, but the tokenizers are agnostic to what drives them — shows where the engineering went next:

  • T2M-GPT — plain VQ tokens; a compact discrete space that generates well but forces fine detail into a finite codebook.
  • MoMask (2024) — residual vector quantization: several codebooks stacked, each encoding what the previous one missed, which cuts reconstruction error sharply.2
  • 2026 hybrids — DC-Motion keeps discrete tokens for structure and a continuous residual for detail; causal tokenizers stream; language-guided tokenizers shape the codebook toward nameable concepts.3

The trade-off the tokenizer literature states outright is one you already know from the chance chapter: a small discrete codebook is easier to compose with but loses detail; a large one keeps detail but stops being a vocabulary. That is gamut sizing — dozens, not hundreds — rediscovered as a reconstruction-error curve.

docs.title: Family two: discovering segments
docs.text:
A pose is not a gesture. A gesture is a span with a beginning and an end, and the second family goes after exactly that boundary problem — unsupervised temporal segmentation of skeleton streams.

The 2025 method to know is skeleton motion words.4 A sequence-to-sequence temporal autoencoder learns a latent representation that keeps the joints disentangled; the latent sequence is cut into short patches and quantized, yielding discrete "motion words"; clustering the words then recovers semantically meaningful action segments — without labels, and without anyone deciding the segment length in advance. A 2026 successor makes the quantization hierarchical across space and time, so coarse units decompose into finer ones — a first, data-driven hint at the unit/modifier layering the gamut chapter built by hand.5 Beneath these sit the earlier rungs: Motion2Language's unsupervised segmentation synchronized to language, frame-wise discrete-feature structure extraction, and the classic hidden-Markov-model and hierarchical-clustering primitive-discovery work of the 2000s and 2010s.6 None of it is dance-specific; all of it runs on the skeleton streams dance capture produces.

docs.title: What the machines keep rediscovering
docs.text:
Step back from the two families and a pattern jumps out that should feel familiar by now. Every one of these systems that generates well has re-derived the two-layer architecture of the chance chapter from data: a codebook — small, finite, inspectable, the gamut — plus a sequencer (a GPT, a masked transformer) that decides only continuity. Bailando's "selecting and sorting units" is Cunningham's charts with the charts learned. Nobody set out to rebuild the gamut+sequencer split; it's what works.

And the same step back shows exactly what the machines do not supply — which is the list of everything a gamut needs beyond a pile of clusters:

  • Names. Codes are indices. A dancer cannot be told "do 47."
  • Type signatures. No code carries pre- and postconditions; legality is learned implicitly by the sequencer, which means it can't be checked, only trusted.
  • The unit boundary. Is the unit a pose, a patch, a phrase? Each family picks a granularity by architecture, and the choice is a design decision no model makes for you.
  • Performability. A frequently recurring cluster is not thereby a masterable unit — it may be a transition, an artifact of the capture, or a fragment of something larger.

Each of those is a job the architecture chapter assigned to the human tier, and discovery leaves every one of them there.

docs.title: How you'd know a discovered vocabulary is good
docs.text:
There is no standard evaluation — which is itself useful to know, because it means you get to assemble one from first principles, and the principles are already in this part:

  • Coverage — score the clusters against an independent class list; Guest's Movement Alphabet is sitting right there as the checklist. Empty cells tell you what the corpus, or the method, can't see.
  • Stability — the same vocabulary should reappear across random seeds and across different corpora of the same style; a vocabulary that changes every run is noise with labels.
  • Interpretability and performability — can a dancer name the centroid of each cluster and perform it? This is a human check, and it's decisive.
  • Downstream — does generating over the codebook beat generating over raw poses? If the units don't help the sequencer, they aren't units.
  • Size — a usable vocabulary lands in the dozens. A 512-entry codebook is a feature space, not a gamut, until it has been clustered again — and that second clustering is where taste re-enters.

docs.title: What it would take
docs.text:
Put the pieces together and a working discovery pipeline is not speculative — it is a sequence of existing components with a human gate in the right place:

  1. Capture dance video into world-grounded skeletons (GVHMR for archival footage, FreeMocap for your own room).
  2. Discover candidates with both families — a pose codebook for the unit-pose layer, motion words for segments — and keep the candidate count generous.
  3. Cluster down to dozens with the Movement Alphabet as coverage scorer, so the result spans rather than clusters around whatever the corpus over-represents.
  4. Gate: a dancer or choreographer names each candidate, performs it, and prunes — the machine clusters, the human decides what is a unit.
  5. Type the survivors with pre/post signatures (support, level, balance, momentum, facing, free limbs) and build the legality graph.

Discovery, in other words, is best understood as a proposal generator for a gamut — it replaces the blank page, not the choreographer. That's a real gain: the blank page is where hand-built vocabularies cluster around one taste, and a model that has watched a thousand hours proposes cells the author would never have filled. It also reframes the latent-spaces chapter: a codebook is precisely a latent space discretized into a gamut — the hybrid position that chapter argued was the interesting one, with the discretization now learned.

Several of these threads deserve their own deep dives — one per method family, and one on the evaluation recipe — and they're queued. For now the map is the point: you can see exactly how far the machines get, and exactly where the choreographer is still standing.

  4. Skeleton Motion Words for Unsupervised Skeleton-Based Temporal Action Segmentation (2025). ↩

docs.title: Technique as vocabulary
docs.text:
The previous chapter ended on the cost of a lexicon: it quietly decides what is thinkable. Modern dance is what happened when a generation of American and European choreographers found ballet's vocabulary unthinkable for them — wrong body, wrong subjects, wrong relationship to gravity — and, instead of extending the word-list, did something structurally stranger: each built a technique, a daily training system that produces a body with particular capacities and tendencies, and let that trained body be the vocabulary.

The distinction is worth holding precisely. Ballet stores its vocabulary in names — a lexicon any trained body can execute. A modern technique stores its vocabulary in the instrument itself: train Graham technique for a decade and your torso can do things — and reaches for things — that an equally virtuosic ballet body doesn't. Three storage formats for movement vocabulary run through this whole subject: the name-list, the trained body, and (held for later) the operator set. This chapter is the second one.

docs.title: Graham: the dramatic torso
docs.text:
Martha Graham's technique is built on one mechanical seed: contraction and release. The contraction is a deep, breath-initiated hollowing of the torso — pelvis curling under, spine curving, the body's center gripping as if punched or sobbing — and the release is its opening. Add the spiral (rotation organized around the spine) and a deliberate return of dance to the floor — falls, kneels, ground work, at a time when ballet treated the floor as merely what you rise from — and you have an instrument purpose-built for her repertoire's subject matter: Greek tragedy, psychological extremity, desire and dread made muscular.

The historical irony: by the time of her death the "rebellion" was a syllabus. Graham technique is taught worldwide with named exercises in fixed sequence — bounces, breathings, spirals, pleadings — as codified as anything in the Vaganova method. A technique that produces a distinctive body becomes a lexicon over time, because pedagogy demands units. Codification, apparently, is less a choice than a fate.

docs.title: Humphrey and Limón: the body as pendulum
docs.text:
Doris Humphrey — Graham's great contemporary, and the author of the craft bible the best practices chapter leans on — seeded her technique differently: fall and recovery, which she framed as the drama of movement itself, "the arc between two deaths." The vertical stillness of perfect balance and the horizontal stillness of collapse are both inert; everything alive happens between them — the yielding to gravity, the catch, the rebound, the suspension at the top of the arc where weight goes briefly silent. Weight, breath rhythm, swing, momentum: the technique trains a body that rides physics rather than defying it (ballet's whole aesthetic of effortless verticality being precisely the defiance).

Her dancer José Limón built the now-dominant refinement — Limón technique — organizing the same physics around breath and the sensation of weight moving through body parts in succession. For a builder of movement systems the Humphrey–Limón line is the important one, because it puts momentum and gravity into the vocabulary itself — exactly the state the gamut chapter insisted must be first-class, discovered here as an aesthetic rather than an annotation.

docs.title: Cunningham: the chance-ready body
docs.text:
Merce Cunningham's technique reads differently once you know (from the chance chapter) what it was for. He needed dancers who could survive his sequencer: any movement following any other, continuity decided by hexagram. So the technique manufactures the necessary affordances: a strong vertical ballet-like leg base underneath a spine treated as a limb — his phrase — with the torso trained through enumerated positions (upright, curve, arch, twist, tilt) that could be recombined with any step, any direction, any rhythm. Clarity over expressivity; every direction equally "front" (chance decides facing, so the body must be omnidirectional); no movement allowed to depend on an emotional preparation, because its neighbor tomorrow might be anything.

It is the clearest case in dance history of a technique reverse-engineered from a compositional system — the training exists so that the generator's output is performable. Any synthetic-dance pipeline contains the same dependency, usually undeclared: what the generator may emit is bounded by what the executing instrument was trained on.

docs.title: Release and contact: subtracting the vocabulary
docs.text:
The postmodern generation — Judson and after — turned the critique inward: if Graham's technique encodes Graham's drama in every trained torso, then technique itself is a style you can't take off. Two responses became traditions of their own.

Release technique — descending from Mabel Todd's The Thinking Body through Skinner Releasing and into the training of most contemporary dancers today — trains subtraction: skeletal alignment, efficiency, imagery ("the skull floats"), letting go of held tension, so that movement arrives with minimal stylistic residue. A body trained to be less marked — the pedestrian, unforced look that defines so much contemporary European stage dance descends from this.

Contact improvisation, initiated by Steve Paxton in 1972, removes the vocabulary's other pillar: pre-composition. Two bodies share weight through a rolling point of contact, and the material is whatever physics offers — falls, lifts, counterbalances — discovered live, never fixed. There are trainable skills (giving weight, following the contact point, falling safely) but deliberately no steps. It survives worldwide as a practice with no repertoire at all: the limiting case of technique-as-vocabulary, where the vocabulary has been dissolved entirely into capacity.

docs.title: Gaga: the anti-vocabulary with a vocabulary problem
docs.text:
The most discussed contemporary case is Gaga, Ohad Naharin's movement language, developed at Batsheva Dance Company. Its classes ban mirrors, visitors, and demonstration-and-copy; instead a teacher speaks a continuous stream of sensation images — float, quake, melt, groove, flesh hanging on bone, effort traveling to the fingertips — and dancers research the sensations in their own bodies, never converging on a shared shape.1 It is explicitly an anti-vocabulary: no named positions, no correct form, nothing to copy.

And yet: Batsheva dancers are recognizable across a stage in seconds — the loosed spines, the grounded volatility, the fast redistribution of effort. Refusing shape-names while training shared sensation-names simply relocates the vocabulary one layer down, from geometry to texture. (The reader of the effort chapter will recognize the layer: Gaga's words live on roughly the axis Laban factored — quality, not position.) The honest summary is that Gaga is a codified vocabulary of qualities with an enforced norm against codifying shapes — a fascinating data point that the vocabulary layer is inescapable, and the only real choice is which layer you name.

docs.title: Forsythe: the vocabulary of operations
docs.text:
The third storage format, previewed. William Forsythe's Improvisation Technologies trains neither names nor a particular body but a set of operations — extend a line, fold it, extrude it, avoid it, reorient it — applicable to any material the dancer already has. A dancer literate in the ~thirty operations carries a generative system, not a repertoire; aim it at ballet vocabulary (Forsythe's own dancers were classical) and you get his hyperextended, off-axis deconstructions; aim it at pedestrian movement and you get something else entirely.

The gamut chapter treated this catalog as engineering material — the operator layer, with its tiers and closure rules. Seen from this chapter's angle it is the endpoint of a century's argument: vocabulary stored as names (ballet), then as bodies (Graham to Gaga), then as transformations — which is, not coincidentally, the layer a machine can hold most naturally, and the doorway to the latent-space question of whether the material itself can go continuous.

docs.title: The lesson for instrument-builders
docs.text:
Every technique in this chapter is a claim shaped like: train these capacities daily, and a recognizable movement world becomes available. Abstract one step and it applies to any generative instrument: the training regime is a vocabulary decision. A model's "technique" is its corpus and objectives — what it practiced daily — and its affordances and habits follow from that as surely as the Graham torso follows from the bounces. Cunningham had to invent a technique so his generator's output would be performable; builders of synthetic dancers inherit the same problem with the arrow reversed: the generator's habits are set by what its body of training could do. Choose the practice, and you have — silently — chosen the style.

Field notes

No commons notes rendered directly — general-knowledge background, per the sourcing policy. It motivates the technique-side reading of structure-operator-mechanizability-tiers (Forsythe as literacy) and sets up the corpus-as-technique framing that systems/latent-spaces.md develops.

  1. Naharin developed Gaga partly through rehabilitating his own back injury; the practice now runs in parallel tracks — Gaga/dancers and Gaga/people, the latter for untrained movers, which is itself evidence of how little the method depends on a shape lexicon. The documentary Mr. Gaga (2015) shows the classes. ↩

docs.text: TRAVELLING cross the floor · go DIRECTION gesture into a line of space

MOTION TOWARD defined by its approach MOTION AWAY defined by its departure DESTINATION defined by where it ends RELATING defined by its relationship

Solid cards: the ten performable verb classes. Dashed cards: not performables — ways of specifying a movement (by approach, departure, endpoint, relationship) plus the wildcard. docs.title: The captured body: video to skeleton to animation
docs.text:
Part VII begins here, pulled forward by a practical question: if you point a camera at a dancer — or at seventy years of dance footage — what can you actually extract, with what tools, at what cost, and how do you make the extracted skeleton move like a person instead of like a haunted marionette? This chapter maps the pipeline end to end as it stands in mid-2026, with particular attention to the two things worth caring about most: what's genuinely free, and the increasingly clever machinery — learned priors, physics simulation — that separates plausible animation from sliding, jittering approximation.1

The pipeline has five stages, and it helps to name them up front, because tools slot into stages, not into the whole:

video → 2D keypoints → 3D body in world space → cleanup → retarget to a rig → render

docs.title: The interchange body: SMPL
docs.text: First, the format that makes the ecosystem hang together. Nearly all current research emits SMPL (or its hands-and-face extension SMPL-X): a parametric human body — a fixed-topology mesh driven by per-joint rotations plus a handful of shape parameters. It matters to you for one reason: it is the lingua franca. Pose estimators emit it, motion generators consume it, converters to FBX and Blender exist and are boring. When evaluating any tool in this space, "can it get to SMPL?" is the portability question, the way "can it export stems?" is in audio.

docs.title: Stage one: 2D keypoints
docs.text: Per-frame 2D pose detection is mature, fast, and free — MediaPipe's 33-landmark body, and the RTMPose/DWPose family that produces the colored-limb skeletons your video-generation stack already consumes as control input. Two things worth knowing: 2D is done as a research problem for ordinary footage (the interesting failures are all downstream), and 2D alone is already useful — a DWPose skeleton drives pose-conditioned video generation directly, no 3D lift required. The 3D stages below exist for when you need the body, not just the picture of one: editing, retargeting, physics, or building a motion corpus.

docs.title: Stage two: the lift, and the world-grounding problem
docs.text:
Lifting 2D detections to a 3D body was never really the hard part per-frame; the hard part is world grounding — recovering the global trajectory and orientation so that a dancer who travels, turns, and jumps does so in the world instead of swimming in place at the camera's origin. This is precisely the dance-relevant half: travel and facing are choreography.

The state of the art (single ordinary camera, no markers, no suit):

  • WHAM (CVPR 2024) made world grounding respectable — motion context plus learned foot-contact cues to pin trajectory to the ground.2
  • GVHMR (SIGGRAPH Asia 2024; TPAMI 2026) is the current default. Its trick is a coordinate system: predict pose in gravity-view coordinates — a frame defined by gravity plus the camera ray, uniquely inferable per image — which removes an ambiguity the network otherwise wastes capacity resolving. It emits SMPL-X, grounds camera-space motion more accurately than WHAM, and its core network is roughly seven times faster (~0.28 s vs ~2.0 s); on the standard per-pose accuracy benchmark the two are within a fraction of a millimeter.3
  • OnlineHMR (CVPR 2026) does the same job causally — streaming, for live settings.

All of this is research code: free on GitHub, real to run (a GPU, a Python environment, no support desk), and worth it when you want the best monocular result on footage you don't control — archival dance video being the canonical case.

When you do control the room, triangulate instead. Multiple cheap cameras beat one clever network. FreeMocap — free and open source — turns two or more ordinary webcams into a markerless rig: MediaPipe's 553 landmarks per frame (body, both hands, face) triangulated into 3D, exported to native Blender, FBX, or CSV; its April 2026 release added reprojection-outlier rejection, so one badly placed camera no longer corrupts the whole solve.4 Its sibling Pose2Sim takes any camera mix (phones, GoPros) into an OpenSim biomechanical skeleton — the tool when joint kinematics need to be right, not just plausible-looking.5

docs.title: What dance does to all of this
docs.text:
Dance is close to a worst case for capture, and the failure modes are specific enough to plan around:6

  • Floorwork breaks the priors. Standing-biased pose priors and foot-contact heuristics misfire when weight is on the back, side, or hands — the same standing bias the notation systems carry, now baked into models trained on walking-heavy data. Rolls and inversions are where monocular methods hallucinate hardest; multi-camera capture is the honest fix.
  • Spins flip orientation. Left/right ambiguity under fast rotation produces the characteristic snap where the body turns 180° between frames. (Recall that near-symmetric skeletons carry limb identity almost entirely in subtle appearance cues — at speed, those cues blur away.)
  • Fast motion blurs and jumps. Large inter-frame displacement defeats tracking; power moves defeat it so thoroughly that BRACE — the breakdancing dataset — had to be partly annotated by hand because automatic capture failed on exactly the material it exists to cover. Shoot 60 fps or better for anything percussive.
  • Costume occludes. Skirts, coats, long hair, hats — everything the staged-body chapters will celebrate is an occlusion generator. Capture passes want fitted clothing; wardrobe is a render-time decision, which pose-conditioned video generation happily accommodates.

The standard benchmark, incidentally, is AIST++: 5.2 hours, 1,408 sequences, ten genres, multi-view with known cameras — worth knowing both as a corpus and as the substrate most music-to-dance generation is trained on.7

docs.title: The clever part: making it move like a person
docs.text:
Raw output from every one of these systems shares a look: feet that skate, joints that jitter, poses that are individually fine and collectively boneless. The repair techniques are where the field has gotten genuinely clever, and they sort into three tiers by what the fix can see — a tiering worth internalizing because it recurs everywhere in this territory.

Tier one: geometric patches. Detect foot-contact frames from velocity and height, then pin the foot with inverse kinematics for the contact's duration; filter the jitter. Cheap, local, ships as a checkbox in commercial tools ("foot locking"). It fixes the single most visible artifact and nothing else — and a pin that fights the data can buy you a knee pop in exchange for the slide.

Tier two: learned priors — denoising by projection. Train a generative model of how humans actually move — VPoser for single poses, HuMoR for whole trajectories, motion-diffusion models as the current generation — then pull noisy estimates toward what the model believes.8 Readers of the latent-spaces chapter will recognize this instantly: it is the manifold, used as a repair strategy — off-manifold capture gets projected back onto the thin surface of plausible human movement. And it inherits the manifold's caveat with teeth: a prior is only as good as its corpus's coverage, so a prior trained on walking-heavy mocap will "correct" your floorwork toward standing. For dance, check what the prior was fed before letting it edit.

Tier three: physics — legalization by embodiment. The deepest fix, and the one most worth understanding. Train a reinforcement-learning controller that drives a simulated humanoid — mass, joint limits, friction, gravity — to track your noisy reference motion: the DeepMimic line (2018) through AMP to PHC (Perpetual Humanoid Control), the current workhorse, which tracks large noisy corpora robustly.9 The output is whatever the simulated body actually did — and therefore feet cannot slide (friction is real), momentum is conserved, balance is kept or visibly lost. Physics repairs what the other tiers cannot even represent: forces, weight, contact — precisely the fields the gamut chapter called the treacherous ones, and pedagogy's root cause of transition failure. Seen from this subject's angle, tier three is the legality graph gone continuous: simulation as a checker that cannot be argued with. The costs: an RL training loop, and a subtle one — the controller is itself a performer with an accent, and extreme stylization comes back slightly flattened. Sound familiar? It's the LifeForms lesson again: every tool's easy path shows up in the output.

The tiers compose — prior-then-physics is the strong pipeline — and choosing by failure mode keeps it cheap: skating feet, tier one; jitter and odd poses, tier two; impossible dynamics or contact-rich floorwork, tier three.

And there's an interactive version of the whole idea. Cascadeur — a standalone keyframe animator with a genuinely usable free tier — packages the priors inside the authoring loop rather than as after-the-fact repair: AutoPosing completes a natural pose from a few dragged handles (a learned pose prior as a direct-manipulation tool), and AutoPhysics nudges keyframed motion toward ballistic and momentum correctness while preserving the animator's intent.10 It is, in this subject's vocabulary, a human gate with a physics-literate assistant — worth knowing even if your pipeline is mostly generative, because it's the fastest way to hand-fix the ten seconds the pipeline got wrong.

docs.title: Stage five: retargeting, the quiet quality-killer
docs.text: Captured motion lands on your character through retargeting — mapping one skeleton's motion onto another's proportions — and this unglamorous step is where free pipelines usually lose their realism. Different limb lengths shift contact timing; a clean capture retargeted carelessly skates again. The free path is settled: Blender (with Rokoko's free plugin or native tooling) and Mixamo for auto-rigging; Cascadeur's retargeting sits in its paid tier. Budget a cleanup pass after every retarget, and treat rig choice as an aesthetic decision — proportions are style, as anyone who has watched the same motion on two differently-built dancers already knows.

docs.title: What this opens
docs.text:
Two doors, both of which later chapters walk through. Capture turns footage into corpus — the raw material for learned movement spaces and for the unsupervised gesture-discovery program (chapter 10's research sweep, coming) starts as exactly these skeletons. And capture turns performance into control signal: a cleaned 3D take, re-rendered from any angle through the pose-conditioned video pipeline, is the bridge between a real dancer's phrasing and a synthetic dancer's body — the subject of the rendering chapter ahead.
